new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar states that stress (and vowel length) are 'generally non-phonemic' in Girawa, i.e. non-contrastive, but gives no rule for where stress falls. The only positional fact is morphophonemic: when the locative suffix -a attaches to a noun ending in a (mena 'village' + -a), the vowels fuse and the resulting word-final syllable is stressed and lengthened (written mena, glossed 'into/from the village'). Phonology proper is left to the separate SIL papers (Gasaway & Sims 1977 'A preliminary phonology of Girawa', SIL 56088, not online; Lillie 1992 Girawa Organised Phonology Data, SIL 42443, file could not be reached by automated download; Gasaway 1982 'Girawa and natural phonology', SIL 43867, file could not be reached by automated download), none of which is this work.
new_statements.exceptions: locative -a on an a-final word: fused final syllable becomes stressed and long (the one case where stress/length is said to be noticeable); otherwise stress and length 'generally non-phonemic'
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes Girawa (Kokon Family, Mabuso Stock), data from Sai village (June 1976-Nov 1977, Gasaway & Sims) plus area-wide data 1980-Feb 1992 (Lillie); it notes i/u fluctuation 'between the dialects of the language' (sec. 2.1) but treats one variety. The Lillie 1989 thesis (not opened) is on the same language by the same fieldworker.

tone.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is not phonemic. It is ambivalent in shorter words and predictable in longer words. In longer words the main stress falls on the last syllable, and in shorter words the position of the stress fluctuates although some words seem to have a preferred stress.

sources.note: Record only + secondhand: the fullest phonological description of Girawa (41 pp); Clifton 1988:47 quotes its p.24 on vowel clusters ('those clusters with a high vowel /i, u/ as second member have a single beat of prominence, while those with a high vowel as first member have two beats of prominence'); a suprasegmental section (stress, probably a remark on tone/intonation) is expected but unseen; the later OPD (1992) and Gasaway 1982, both based on it, report no tone.
